parsed_answer.content:
When dealing with character-based input streams in Java, developers frequently choose between BufferedReader and Scanner. Understanding the architectural differences between these two utilities is critical for writing high-performance I/O applications. BufferedReader, introduced in JDK 1.0, is a synchronous, buffered wrapper around a Reader that is explicitly designed to read text from a character-input stream efficiently by buffering characters to minimize expensive underlying OS-level read operations. It operates primarily on lines of text, reading into an internal char array buffer (typically 8KB by default) and treating everything as raw strings.

On the other hand, Scanner, introduced later in JDK 1.5, is a text scanner that can parse primitive types and strings using regular expressions. Scanner breaks its input down into tokens using a delimiter pattern, which defaults to whitespace. While this makes Scanner exceptionally convenient for parsing console input or structured files containing mixed types (like integers, floats, and strings), it introduces a heavy performance penalty due to regex compilation, token matching, and lack of thread-safety. BufferedReader is synchronized on its reader lock for thread safety (though typically used within a single thread), whereas Scanner is entirely unsynchronized and unsafe for concurrent access.

rows: Slower due to regex matching and tokenization

items: BufferedReader maintains an internal 8KB char array buffer. When a read() or readLine() request is made, it checks if the buffer has data remaining. If empty, it triggers a single bulk read(char[] cbuf, int offset, int length) on the underlying Reader, drastically reducing system call overhead.

Scanner uses a Matcher and a Pattern engine to parse tokens. Even simple calls like nextInt() involve regular expression compilation and matching states, causing significant CPU overhead and garbage collection pressure due to frequent intermediate object allocations.

Scanner masks underlying IOExceptions by catching them internally and setting an internal exception state, which can be retrieved using the ioException() method. BufferedReader forces the developer to explicitly catch or declare IOExceptions, adhering strictly to Java's checked exception contract.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production gotcha occurs when mixing Scanner with BufferedReader on standard input (System.in). Scanner can leave trailing newline characters in the input buffer because it uses whitespace delimiters, causing subsequent BufferedReader.readLine() calls to immediately return empty strings. Furthermore, always favor BufferedReader when processing large files or competitive programming inputs where throughput is paramount; switch to Scanner only when interactive parsing of mixed primitive types from trusted, small inputs is required.

title: What is the difference between BufferedReader and Scanner?
